image.alt: The white Calm Tech Certified mark appears at the center of a black background, introducing the Institute's certification program and 81-point criteria.

slides.text:
How should we judge
a good technology?

The Calm Tech Institute evaluates how a product treats human attention and the surrounding environment through 81-point criteria. What is publicly available is six evaluation areas and a certification process.

image.alt:
What is published matters more
than the number 81

slides.text:
What is published matters more
than the number 81

The Institute's official term is ‘81-point criteria.’ Its public pages, however, do not list all 81 questions or the complete scoring rubric.

What can be verified is the process—evaluation, score and feedback, then a certification decision—and six areas: attention, periphery, durability, light, sound, and materials. We should not fill the unpublished parts with guesses.

image.alt: A person sits on a sofa and checks a Fairphone lock screen with both hands. The image illustrates attention demands and is not presented as a Calm Tech certification case.

slides.text:
First, does the product support
attention—or take it away?

The attention area asks whether a product works with human focus or repeatedly breaks it. If every state becomes a pop-up or badge, people return to the screen without being able to judge what matters.

The question is not simply whether there are fewer alerts, but __whether the signal becomes clear only when action is actually required__.

image.alt: A blue ring glows on a black Amazon Echo on a dark wooden table, showing a peripheral signal that communicates device status without a screen.

slides.text:
Second, can you understand its state
without looking at a screen?

The periphery area asks whether people can perceive a product's state without fixing their gaze on it. A change in light, a short sound, vibration, or movement can let information remain in the background most of the time.

The signal still needs meaning, not decoration. It should distinguish __what changed and whether action is needed now__.

image.alt: A technician in protective glasses inspects cables and electronic equipment at a workbench, illustrating repair, failure behavior, and customer support.

slides.text:
Third, does it still support you
when something fails?

The durability area looks at how a product fails and what support remains afterward. A product that loses every basic function when a network or one feature stops working creates more uncertainty for the user.

Repair, support, and fallback behavior are not merely after-sales service. They are __part of the experience that should be designed from the beginning__.

image.alt: Two hands adjust a control dial on lighting equipment in a dark space. The display shows output values, illustrating the sensory effects of light, sound, and materials.

slides.text:
Fourth, sensory burden
is part of product responsibility

The remaining three areas are light, sound, and materials. They ask whether light feels warm or harshly blue, whether moving parts create needless noise, and what materials people touch and live with.

A product may function correctly and still keep a room glowing, humming, or physically uncomfortable. __The burden experienced by the body is also part of performance__.

image.alt: A hand holds the thin edge of a reMarkable Paper Pro near its pen tip, illustrating a product experience reviewed and certified by the Calm Tech Institute.

slides.text:
The purpose of evaluation
is improvement, not a seal

The Institute first evaluates a product, then provides a score and specific feedback. Products that meet the criteria can be certified; others receive a roadmap for a future version or update.

reMarkable Paper Pro is a published certification case. Certification does not guarantee focus for every person. It indicates that the product was reviewed through a defined perspective—and should be treated as a starting point.

image.alt:
When choosing your next product,
what standard would you put
__before the number of features?__

caption.body: The Calm Tech Institute says it evaluates products against 81-point criteria, but it does not publish every individual question or the full scoring rubric. What is public is a six-part framework—attention, periphery, durability, light, sound, and materials—and a process of evaluation, scoring and feedback, followed by certification or an improvement roadmap. The framework asks not how many features a product has, but what relationship it creates with attention, the senses, and failure.
